findings.claim: The paper fixes tau=0.1 for every model, but its own Figure 8 shows the Query-Aware head count varying from 1 to 19 across task and length. Doubling tau to 0.2 raises the count by 6x to 18x. How many heads use the more expensive and less structured Query-Aware path is therefore data-dependent. It is also sensitive to a threshold that was never calibrated per model.
findings.mechanism: D_JS is a continuous quantity compared against a hard cutoff. If many heads have D_JS clustered near the cutoff, small changes in task, length or tau flip many heads. Pooled-estimate accuracy generally depends on the attention distribution, which depends on content and length. Fig. 8 reports Query-Aware counts of 13, 2, 19 and 1 at tau=0.1 for the four task/length panels (a)–(d). At tau=0.2 the panels (e)–(h) read 111, 11, 58 and 18. The same threshold therefore yields very different head mixes by input. Table 6 shows LLaMA at tau=0.3 dropping to 88.38 average and 75.96 at 128k, against 89.18 and 79.09 at tau=0.1. The authors attribute this to admitting heads with inaccurate estimates. Model-specific transfer of 0.1 is likewise unverified.
conditions: D_JS values of many heads fall near 0.1 to 0.2.
Deployment inputs differ from RULER and InfiniteBench in task type or length distribution.
Per-model attention statistics differ enough that 0.1 is not equivalently strict.

findings.claim: Algorithm 4 ranks all (query-block x key-block) scores in one flattened list and stops when the global sum reaches gamma. Equation 3 and its Appendix A rationale require coverage of at least gamma for every query position. These are different stopping rules, so individual query blocks can be left below gamma.
findings.mechanism: If rows of the pooled map are each softmax-normalized and then jointly renormalized, every row carries equal mass. Selecting the largest entries globally still favors rows with peaked distributions. Rows with flat distributions have small per-entry values and are picked last. With a global cutoff, a peaked query block can reach full coverage using few key blocks. A flat query block may get only a fraction of the blocks it needs to reach gamma. This is a different optimization target from the per-query one in Eq. 3.
conditions: Query blocks in the head have heterogeneous peakedness.
The cutoff gamma is low enough that the global cumulative sum stops before flat rows are reached.
Floor mechanisms (first/last key blocks, 1024-token minimum) do not already cover the flat rows' needs.

findings.claim: The Vertical-Slash fallback chooses lines at token granularity, but the kernel runs on 128-sized blocks. Scattered vertical columns or slash offsets can therefore touch many more blocks than the token count suggests, so the real compute fraction can exceed the line budget. The paper reports no measure of block-level versus token-level density for this path.
findings.mechanism: Block-sparse GPU kernels typically compute a whole tile whenever any selected (query, key) position falls inside it. Isolated token columns and diagonals that cross many tiles therefore activate many tiles. Because lines are scored per token while the Triton kernel works with block_size = 128, the realized fraction of computed blocks can be well above the fraction of selected tokens. The O(αn²d) cost model in the appendix does not say which granularity α refers to.
conditions: Selected vertical columns are not clustered within the same key blocks.
The kernel computes whole blocks when any token in the block is selected.
Reported sparsity or alpha is counted at token level.

findings.claim: Because the budget varies with the prompt, attention compute at the same context length differs by task. The reported latency figures are averages over a single attention head and over lengths, so they do not show whether the average speedup survives in batched serving tail latency.
findings.mechanism: In a batched or pipelined server, step time is set by the slowest request or the most loaded head or kernel. Averages of per-call latency do not bound p99. Figure 10 reports total sparsity of 79.83 for 64k task A and 85.72 for 64k task B, at the same context length. If sparsity is 20 and 14 percent density respectively, that is roughly a 1.4x difference in computed attention at a fixed length. Together with per-head variation, this implies content-dependent latency and possible load imbalance. The paper reports only per-head averages, so tail behavior under mixed prompts is not characterized.
conditions: requests of differing difficulty are batched or share a synchronization point
per-head kernel launches are unevenly loaded
tail latency (p99 TTFT) is the metric of interest

findings.claim: Eq. 3 states the coverage constraint per query position (for all i). The Query-Aware implementation (Algorithm 4) flattens the whole block-pooled map and stops once the global sum reaches gamma. That does not ensure each query block's own mass reaches gamma, so the per-row premise of the Appendix A error bound is not enforced by the code path.
findings.mechanism: In general, a global cumulative-mass cutoff over a matrix normalized to sum to 1 places no lower bound on the mass captured within any single row. Rows that hold little of the total pooled mass can be left under-covered while rows that hold more are over-covered. Algorithm 4 flattens and normalizes the pooled map over all (query block, key block) pairs and takes the top entries until the global sum reaches gamma. Row-level coverage is therefore not guaranteed, and the per-row bound (1 - a_S) * sum|v_j| need not hold for every query block. Block-level mass is also not token-level mass.
conditions: Row masses in the pooled map are uneven across query blocks
The 1024-token minimum and the retained first/last key blocks do not already supply adequate coverage for the under-covered rows
The head takes the Query-Aware path, not the Vertical-Slash path

findings.claim: The Appendix A reduction only shows that maximizing captured mass shrinks an upper bound of the form (1 - a_S) * sum_j |v_j|. That bound has a factor summed over all L keys, so for a fixed gamma it can grow with context length. The paper's derivation therefore does not certify that gamma = 0.9 or 0.95 keeps output error controlled at 512k as it does at 8k.
findings.mechanism: A bound of the form (1 - a_S) * sum over L terms of |v_j| increases with L when per-token value norms are roughly constant and a_S is fixed. Monotonicity in a_S is the only property the bound provides. Under the worst-case bound, a fixed gamma gives a weaker guarantee at longer L, and the bound is not tight, so it cannot explain why accuracy holds at a given gamma. Any retained accuracy at long context must come from empirical regularities (value and softmax-mass misalignment, sparsity), which the appendix does not analyse.
conditions: The bound is used as the justification for the gamma-based selection rule.
Value norms do not shrink with L.
The worst case is what is being judged.

findings.claim: The Appendix A bound is written in terms of the true normalized attention mass a_S. The algorithms select indices using pooled-query/key block estimates (Query-Aware heads) or scores from only the last block_size queries (Vertical-Slash heads). The theorem therefore transfers to the deployed method only to the extent that estimated mass matches true mass, a link the appendix does not analyse.
findings.mechanism: Average-pooled Q and K scores are not the same as the average of true softmax scores, and a subset of queries is not the full set of rows. A cumulative sum computed on estimates can differ from the true cumulative mass of the same selected set. The 'sum >= gamma' condition is verified on estimated scores. The true mass a_S in the bound can be lower, so the bound's premise is not checked by the system. The paper's own ablation shows the estimation source matters.
conditions: Selection is performed on pooled or subset estimates.
The estimate-to-true gap is not bounded in the appendix.

findings.claim: The rationale derives a per-query constraint and aggregates it over rows. Algorithm 4 instead flattens the whole block-level map and stops when the global sum reaches gamma, so the budget is shared across query blocks. The per-row guarantee the proof supports is therefore not what this head type implements.
findings.mechanism: A single global cumulative threshold over a flattened map can be met by concentrating selections on a few rows with large mass while leaving other rows below gamma. Row-wise normalization of the bound is lost. Under flattening, individual query rows may capture less than gamma of their own mass, so the per-row error bound does not apply row by row. The aggregated objective is only a surrogate for what the code optimizes.
conditions: The Query-Aware path uses the flatten variant.
Rows differ in the concentration of their estimated attention.

findings.claim: The JS test measures agreement between pooled and true attention only for the last 128 queries. The paper then applies the Query-Aware decision to every query in the head. The test is therefore a proxy whose validity for earlier queries is assumed, not checked.
findings.mechanism: Under a causal mask, the last block of queries attends to every key. Earlier query blocks attend to progressively fewer keys, and their attention may be distributed differently. Pooling quality can also vary with position and with the content of the final tokens. A small D_JS on the last block shows that pooling matches true attention for those queries. It does not show the same for queries earlier in the sequence. If a prompt's final block differs in kind from the rest (for example, a short question appended after a long document), a head could be labeled Query-Aware, or kept Vertical-Slash, on evidence that is unrepresentative.
conditions: The head's query-to-key attention differs between the last block and earlier blocks.
The head is classified Query-Aware, or kept Vertical-Slash, based on the last block alone.
The mismatch affects the blocks that carry task-relevant information.

findings.claim: FlexPrefill scores vertical and slash lines using only the final 128 queries. The paper validates this choice on RULER, whose prompts presumably have a particular layout. The evidence therefore supports the last block as a proxy only for that layout. It does not show the block is representative when the decisive content is not near the end.
findings.mechanism: Vertical and slash scores computed from a row subset only reflect what those rows attend to. In a causal prefill, KV states for early tokens are computed from the sparse pattern chosen for the queries at those early positions. If the last 128 queries attend to different keys than earlier queries do (for example, filler at the end and an instruction earlier), the selected vertical lines will favor keys the filler needs. Keys that earlier queries need get lower scores and may be dropped for all rows. The paper evaluates only RULER and InfiniteBench, so this case is untested.
conditions: The prompt layout places the decisive or most-attended content away from the final block.
The affected head is classified as Vertical-Slash, which the paper says is most heads.
Downstream outputs depend on KV states of the affected early or middle tokens.

findings.claim: Algorithm 4 builds and sorts a pooled block map with (n/b)^2 entries. Appendix G's complexity list gives index construction as O(n log n) and attributes it to the representative attention scores, which is the Vertical-Slash route. The listed complexity therefore does not cover the Query-Aware path, and its extra cost grows quadratically in n/b.
findings.mechanism: A pooled map over n/b blocks per side has (n/b)^2 entries, and sorting it costs at least that many operations. This quantity grows quadratically with sequence length. It is not O(n log n) for fixed block size b. For heads routed to the Query-Aware path, index construction cost scales with (n/b)^2 rather than n log n. The Appendix G overhead summary and the Figure 6 latency share therefore apply to the mixed head population, not to this path in isolation.
conditions: A non-trivial fraction of heads take the Query-Aware path.
Context is long enough that (n/b)^2 is large relative to the attention being skipped.
The sort is not fused or cheaply implemented on the GPU.

findings.claim: A head is routed to the Vertical-Slash path whenever its pooled block-attention estimate diverges from the true distribution by at least τ. That test measures estimate reliability, not whether the head's attention is vertical or diagonal. Heads with diffuse, non-line attention can end up with lines imposed on them.
findings.mechanism: A large Jensen-Shannon distance between pooled and true block attention can come from many causes, such as fine-grained intra-block structure or flat distributions. Only some of these causes produce vertical or slash lines. The routing rule is a binary comparison of dJS against τ, with the else branch set to vertical_slash. The paper's Figure 8 finding that most heads use Vertical-Slash is therefore partly a product of the routing rule. It is not independent evidence that those heads have line structure. The paper itself notes Query-Aware heads can also look vertical-slash, so the correspondence between the label and the structure is loose in both directions.
conditions: Some heads fail the pooled test for reasons unrelated to line structure.
Those heads have attention spread beyond a few verticals and slashes.
The head matters for the task output.

findings.claim: In Table 10 the 1024-token floor gives a large gain at gamma 0.9 but is neutral or negative on average for LLaMA at gamma 0.95. Several long-context cells at 0.95 are worse with the floor. The floor therefore looks like a gamma-coupled rescue mechanism, not a uniform improvement.
findings.mechanism: A per-head token floor only changes the computation for heads whose cumulative-attention selection would otherwise fall below the floor. When gamma is high, fewer heads fall below it. Table 10 shows a large floor effect at gamma 0.9 (LLaMA avg 84.78 without floor vs 88.38 with 1024; GLM 85.26 vs 88.58). At gamma 0.95 the effect is small and mixed. LLaMA avg is 89.42 without floor vs 89.18 with 1024, with 32k at 92.31 vs 89.42 and 64k at 85.34 vs 82.93. GLM avg is 88.82 vs 89.34. The Section 4.3 phrase 'enhances performance' is stated without the gamma boundary that Appendix F.5 gives.
conditions: The floor binds on a fraction of heads that grows as gamma decreases.
Per-cell differences of a few points at gamma 0.95 are noise-level, so the sign of the 0.95 effect is uncertain.

findings.claim: The dynamic budget is chosen per head and per prompt as the smallest set whose estimated attention mass reaches gamma. Reaching that mass does not ensure the head's function is preserved. The paper itself needs an extra minimum-budget floor to stop some heads from collapsing at lower gamma.
findings.mechanism: Attention-mass coverage is a proxy for output fidelity. The Appendix A bound, (1 - a_S) * sum|v_j|, is only an upper bound, and it grows with context length. In Algorithm 3, mass is estimated from the last block_size queries, not from every query. If mass coverage were sufficient, the minimum-budget floor would not be needed. Because a floor is needed when gamma is small, the mass criterion alone can leave some heads under-provisioned. Gamma therefore bounds estimated coverage, not per-prompt accuracy.
conditions: gamma is small enough that some heads fall below a workable token count
the selected indices are evaluated against the true attention mass, not the block-pooled or representative-query estimate
no minimum-budget floor is applied

findings.claim: The paper fixes gamma per model (0.9 for Yi and Qwen, 0.95 for LLaMA and GLM) and presents it as a speed-accuracy knob. Gamma only sets a target for retained attention mass. The paper never states an accuracy-loss tolerance that the chosen gamma is meant to satisfy. How the values were selected is not described. Whether they transfer to other models, tasks or lengths is not tested.
findings.mechanism: A cumulative-attention-mass threshold is a proxy for output fidelity. The paper's own bound in Appendix A scales as (1 - a_S) times the sum of |v_j| over all L positions, so the same retained mass can allow a larger worst-case error as L grows or as value norms change. How much task-relevant signal sits in the dropped mass depends on the model and the task. A gamma that gives near-parity on one model may give a larger loss on another. Table 1 is consistent with this. At gamma 0.9, Yi scores 76.32 against 79.49 for full attention (about 3.2 points lower). GLM at gamma 0.9 is 88.58 against 89.06 (Table 3), and LLaMA at 0.9 is 88.38 against 88.70. Because no loss target is stated, 'near full attention' is not defined by the paper. The values are consistent with having been picked on the reporting benchmark, but the paper does not say how they were picked.
conditions: The model's attention concentration differs from that of the model on which the gamma sweep was run (LLaMA-3.1).
Task-relevant information lies in the tail of the attention distribution that gamma discards.

findings.claim: At a lower gamma, heads with very peaked estimated attention can receive a tiny selected set, and the gamma rule alone does not prevent this. The reported results rely on a separate 1024-token floor and forced first/last key blocks, so the observed accuracy reflects gamma coupled with those rules and not gamma alone.
findings.mechanism: In general, a mass-cutoff rule picks the smallest set reaching the threshold, so a head with a sharp distribution can reach it with very few keys. A very small selected set can also be fragile to estimation error in the pooled or representative-query scores. The paper reports that removing the floor at lower gamma hurts a lot: Llama-3.1-8B at gamma = 0.9 averages 84.78 with no floor and 88.38 with a 1024 floor (Table 10). So the adaptive threshold is not self-sufficient. The floor also bounds the speedup at short context, since 1024 tokens is a large share of a 4k prompt. The link from extreme sparsity to head malfunction is the authors' reported explanation.
conditions: Some heads have highly peaked estimated attention so the mass cutoff selects very few keys
Gamma is low enough that those heads' selected sets fall below a functional size
No floor or forced-block rule compensates

findings.claim: The paper explains why larger models need a higher virtual precision p* to match BitMoD ('larger, more heavy-tailed'). It shows no tail statistics for those models, and p* is not monotone in size. The explanation is asserted, not isolated.
findings.mechanism: In general, a ratio-to-baseline metric such as p* (the precision at which method A matches baseline B's PPL) changes with both A's weakness and B's strength. Without tail measurements, size, architecture, training recipe and baseline strength are confounded. p* is defined against BitMoD's per-model PPL, so a model where BitMoD is unusually strong yields a large p* regardless of tails. The reported values are Mistral-7B 4.6 b vs Qwen2.5-7B 4.4 b, Phi-2 (about 2.7B) 4.5 b vs GPT2-XL 4.1 b, and Qwen2.5-14B 5.0 b. Same-size models differ, and Fig. 4 shows tails only for GPT-2 Large. The heavy-tail attribution is therefore a hypothesis, not a result.
conditions: p* depends on a per-model BitMoD target.
The nine models differ in architecture and training as well as size.
No per-model tail statistic is reported.

findings.claim: Algorithm 1 picks each channel's power-of-two scale by maximizing SQNR between the original and the Posit-quantized weights. The paper does not show that this scale also minimizes model loss or output error.
findings.mechanism: SQNR on weights weights every element's reconstruction error equally. Output error depends on how each weight interacts with activations and downstream layers. A scale that lowers average weight error can still give up accuracy on a few high-sensitivity weights. The SQNR-best of the 16 candidates may differ from the perplexity-best candidate, especially for channels with outliers or sensitive weights. The paper uses perplexity for precision allocation (Algorithm 2) but SQNR for scale selection, and does not test whether the two agree.
conditions: Some channels have weights whose importance is very uneven (outliers or activation-sensitive weights).
The SQNR-best and loss-best candidates differ for those channels.
The loss difference is larger than the noise in the perplexity measurement.

findings.claim: Algorithm 1 takes the bit-width n and a candidate set S as inputs, so the SQNR-best scale generally depends on n. Algorithm 2 upgrades channel windows from 4 to 5 bits. The paper does not say whether the scale is re-searched after an upgrade, nor what range the 16 candidates cover.
findings.mechanism: Changing the Posit bit-width changes the number of fraction bits and the regime reach at each magnitude, so the SQNR-maximizing shift can move. Four index bits give 16 candidates, but the paper does not define S or its range. If the scale selected at 4 b is reused for upgraded windows, those windows may be misaligned at 5 b. If it is re-searched, the ΔPPL in Algorithm 2 mixes the effect of extra bits with the effect of a new scale. Either way the stored 4-bit metadata is tied to one (channel, bit-width) pair. Separately, a fixed 16-candidate window may not reach the useful shift for every channel.
conditions: The SQNR-best scale differs between 4 b and 5 b for a meaningful fraction of channels.
The pipeline reuses the 4 b scale or does not re-run Algorithm 1 after upgrade.
Or the candidate set S does not cover the channel's best shift.

findings.claim: Windowing makes one precision per tile feasible in hardware. It does not show that sensitivity is concentrated at window scale, so sensitive channels spread inside a window would be diluted. The paper's evidence for heterogeneity shows variation across windows, not how sensitivity is distributed inside one.
findings.mechanism: A window's measured ΔPPL is an aggregate over all its channels. A window receives one precision, so a few highly sensitive channels in an otherwise insensitive window can only be upgraded together with their neighbours. Fig. 5 is built from window-level cells. It supports profiling at window level over layer level, but it cannot show how much sensitivity is lost to within-window dilution. Table IV compares window-level MPQ only against layer-wise MPQ. The paper rejects finer-grained MPQ as impractical rather than measuring its accuracy, so the accuracy cost of the window constraint is not quantified.
conditions: Sensitive channels are not co-located within windows.
A finer-grained oracle would reach a lower PPL at the same average bits.

findings.claim: Aligning windows to array columns removes per-channel control cost in hardware. Under Algorithm 2 the profiling work grows with the number of windows, which depends on window size and layer width. The paper reports no profiling cost, and it does not say whether the larger Qwen window was chosen to limit that cost.
findings.mechanism: Each ΔPPL measurement needs a model-level evaluation. The number of such evaluations equals the number of windows. For fixed window size, that number grows with total output channels, and for a fixed model it grows as the window shrinks. Window granularity therefore moves cost from per-channel hardware control to offline profiling. Smaller windows give finer allocation but more evaluations, so a given window size trades off resolution against profiling time. The paper does not report profiling time or the number of windows per model, so this trade-off is not quantified.
conditions: Each window requires its own full perplexity evaluation, as in Algorithm 2.
The reported PPL results depend on windows being profiled individually.

findings.claim: The ranking measures each window's gain when it alone is upgraded from the baseline. The allocation then upgrades many windows at once, so the isolated scores need not predict the combined gain or the best top-k set.
findings.mechanism: In a deep network, errors from quantizing different layers interact through the residual stream and later layers. A sensitivity measured with every other window at baseline is therefore a first-order, marginal estimate. It need not add up across windows that are upgraded together. Taking the top k% of windows from this ranking silently assumes the isolated scores are close to additive and stable. If neighboring windows share the same error, the top-ranked windows may be redundant. The ranking is also computed only at the 4 b baseline and is not recomputed as upgrades accumulate.
conditions: Window effects on PPL interact non-additively, for example through shared residual paths or adjacent layers.
The upgraded set is large enough for overlap among its members to matter.

findings.claim: Windows are ranked by their gain from a 4→5 b upgrade, while the allocator and hardware permit precisions from 4 to 8 b. The accuracy evidence only spans the 4–5 b range, so the ranking and the 6–8 b range are not tested together.
findings.mechanism: Quantization error falls roughly geometrically with bits, so the ordering of windows by sensitivity at one bit step need not match the ordering for a larger step. The marginal value of a bit also diminishes. The ranking is built from a single 4→5 b step. The reported experiments sweep only to about 5 b, so use of 6–8 b windows is neither validated nor ranked by any measurement. The Table I claim of fine-grained 4–8 b tunability is therefore backed by accuracy results only in the 4–5 b subrange.
conditions: A use case needs an average precision above roughly 5 b or per-window precisions above 5 b.
Per-window sensitivity ordering changes across bit steps.

findings.claim: Latency is almost exactly proportional to virtual precision in the default setting. This suggests a compute-dominated, zero-intercept regime. Table X shows the advantage shrinking as B and L grow, and the paper does not explain why.
findings.mechanism: End-to-end latency is the sum of P-proportional bit-serial weight compute and terms that do not scale with weight bits, such as activation traffic, attention, KV-cache access, and FP16 rescale or accumulation. The share of the non-P terms depends on batch size and sequence length. From the Fig. 11a PEB values, 0.225 at 4.1 b and 0.274 at 5.0 b give a slope of about 0.054 per bit and an intercept of about 0.002. These points come from different models, so this is only suggestive. The default setting looks nearly purely P-proportional. Table X then shows speedup over BitMoD falling from 1.8x to 1.6x and over FP16 from 4.1x to 3.4x as (B, L) grow to (8, 8192). So the fractional-bit payoff is regime-dependent, and that regime dependence is not shown or explained.
conditions: The latency model has a P-independent component
That component grows with B and L, or P-proportional compute is amortized differently

evidence.support_description: Latency increases nearly linearly with precision
Unless otherwise stated, hardware evaluations use batch size 1 and an input sequence length of 256 tokens.
the original latency-sensitive setting (B=1, L=256)

findings.claim: FlexPosit gives up the calibrated real-valued scale used by conventional group-wise dequantization and allows only powers of two. The scale grid therefore has octave resolution, and any fractional-octave mismatch between a channel and the Posit profile cannot be corrected.
findings.mechanism: A real-valued optimal scale generally falls between two adjacent powers of two. Rounding to the nearest power of two leaves a residual misalignment of up to about half an octave in log2 terms. A residual that large can matter when only 4 to 5 bits are available. For channels whose best real scale is far from a power of two, the quantization error is higher than with a real-valued scale. The hardware saving (exponent-add rescale, 0.4% area per Table IX) is paid for with this loss of scale resolution. How large the loss is depends on how much the tapered Posit profile tolerates the mismatch.
conditions: Per-channel optimal real-valued scales are spread across fractional octaves rather than clustered near powers of two.
Posit(n,1) quantization error is sensitive to a half-octave shift of the distribution.
The low-bit regime leaves little precision margin.

findings.claim: The accounting for storage and fetch of mixed-width windows is not shown. Energy and latency results use the nominal mean bit-width as the cost proxy, while real traffic depends on the packed layout, padding at window boundaries and precision metadata.
findings.mechanism: Off-chip memory is accessed in fixed-size bursts and words. Compact storage of mixed 4-bit and 5-bit streams needs a layout and address map that tracks where each window's payload starts. Effective bytes moved equal payload bits plus padding and metadata. Fractional precision is realized as a time average over windows with integer P. The paper tags the layout 'Aligned' (Table I) and reports a 4 b per-channel scale index. It gives no figure for padding or window-boundary effects, and no cycle or traffic count at precision transitions. Since the stated saving from 4.1 b rather than 5.0 b is small, any unreported overhead of this kind is non-negligible relative to the benefit.
conditions: Window payload size is not a multiple of the memory access granularity
Precision metadata or alignment padding is stored beyond the stated bits

evidence.support_description: All weights in a channel window share the same precision within the 4–8 bit range.
a compact 4 b index stores the selected per-channel scale with low metadata overhead
preserving memory and systolic regularity for LLM edge inference

findings.claim: The shared-accumulator argument for the 4-way MAC cluster holds exactly at the minimum precision P=4. At P>4 each PE finishes a product every P cycles, so the shared accumulator is busy only 4/P of cycles. The text's 'continuously utilized' wording therefore describes only the 4 b point.
findings.mechanism: A bit-serial PE emits one product every P cycles. Four PEs sharing one accumulator then deliver 4 products per P cycles, so the accumulator receives an input in 4 of every P cycles. Beyond P=4 the remaining cycles are idle. This is the same 4/P throughput the paper states for a cluster. Cluster throughput scales as 4/P, and the shared accumulator's idle fraction grows from 0 at P=4 to 50% at P=8. Under iso-PPL operation, models need an average of about 4.1 to 5.0 b, so most FlexPosit windows run at P above 4. The fractional-precision benefit therefore comes with a decline in accumulator utilization that the 'continuously utilized' wording does not convey.
conditions: P>4 for a given window.
The four PEs of a cluster still share one accumulator.

findings.claim: The deadline for token n is a fixed linear schedule from arrival. Slack banked by an early first token or early decodes is spent on larger chunks. A decode request can therefore see inter-token gaps well above the nominal TBT SLO and still count as compliant. A per-token TBT target and a cumulative-deadline check measure different things.
findings.mechanism: Eq. 2 defines D_n = arrival + TTFT + (n-1)*TBT, so every decode request is measured against a cumulative schedule. Finishing the first token early moves the request ahead of that schedule. Any later gap that keeps it behind the D_n line is not a violation. The chunk-size budget is set from min decode slack, which can be large when the first token came early. Under this scheme one batch iteration can then take much longer than 50ms. That produces a gap between consecutive tokens above the TBT target, and it is still deadline-compliant.
conditions: The request's first token arrives well before its TTFT deadline.
The scheduler spends the banked slack on larger chunks.
TBT compliance is computed against D_n rather than against per-gap thresholds.

findings.claim: Dynamic chunking draws on slack from lenient tiers and low load, so its benefit depends on that slack existing. The paper itself shows no gain from dynamic chunking in PD disaggregation, where the baseline chunk is already 8K. Under sustained overload the paper does not show that the chunking gain persists, and its ablation attributes the larger share of overload improvement to relegation.
findings.mechanism: Slack is a consumable quantity. It is produced when prefills finish early and when requests have lenient deadlines, and it is consumed when the system is saturated or strict requests dominate. Raising the chunk past the baseline only helps when there is room above that baseline. The 20% chunking gain is a regime-specific result near optimal load with a small baseline chunk. At high load, chunk sizes plausibly return toward the strict-tier size. That is inferred, since the paper shows chunk traces only for the Az-conv trace over 200 iterations, not under overload. The overload-handling advantage is more plausibly attributable to relegation and prioritization.
conditions: The batch contains at least one strict-tier decode whose slack is nearly exhausted.
The baseline chunk is not already large.
Load is high enough that early prefill completion no longer accumulates slack.

findings.claim: With the reported alpha range (0 to 10 ms/token) and Az-Code prompt lengths, the alpha*remaining-prefill term is far smaller than the gap between the 600s and 1800s tier deadlines. Hybrid prioritization should therefore act mostly as SRPF reordering within a tier, while cross-tier order stays close to EDF. 'Smooth interpolation' holds only when deadlines are close together.
findings.mechanism: A linear key deadline + alpha*tokens reorders two requests only if the alpha*token difference exceeds their deadline difference. Millisecond-per-token coefficients times a few thousand tokens give tens of seconds. Table 3 gives tier deadlines of 6s (TTFT), 600s and 1800s (TTLT). The p90 Az-Code prompt is 6251 tokens (Table 2), so alpha=8 shifts a long request's key by about 50s. That is above the 6s Q1 TTFT deadline but well below the 600s and 1800s tier gaps. Cross-tier overtaking would need arrival-time differences of several hundred seconds. This is an inference from the reported numbers, not something the authors state.
conditions: Deadlines are in seconds and alpha is in ms/token, so the shift is alpha*tokens/1000 seconds.
Prompt lengths stay near the Az-Code distribution (p90 about 6K).
The Table 3 tiers (6s / 600s / 1800s) are used.

findings.claim: Priority uses only the TTFT/TTLT deadline plus remaining work, and the paper says TBT is handled by chunking. The prefill budget C is computed from the minimum slack over all decodes. A tight-slack decode request therefore shrinks the prefill work available to every queued request, and the prefill selector cannot see or weigh this. The stated objective, minimizing violations while maximizing throughput, gives no rule for resolving this tension.
findings.mechanism: Algorithm 1 computes min_decode_slack over all decodes and uses it to get the chunk budget C. The priority comparator uses only arrival, TTFT SLO and remaining prefill tokens. A smaller chunk lowers prefill throughput for the whole queue, including strict-TTFT requests. TTFT and TTLT outcomes are influenced by decode-queue state that the priority function does not model. The priority ordering is therefore not by itself a fix for that effect. The chunk predictor is tuned to under-predict, which can further reduce prefill throughput.
conditions: Many concurrent decodes have small slack.
Interactive requests are waiting in the prefill queue.

findings.claim: Capping the prefill chunk by the minimum decode slack keeps next-token deadlines only to the extent that the learned latency predictor is accurate and errs in one direction for the batch at hand. The paper's reported <10% error margin and its under-prediction bias are not shown to be a worst-case bound.
findings.mechanism: A slack budget expressed in time must be converted into a token budget through a model. Any prediction error in that model translates directly into a possible deadline overshoot. A random forest trained on profiled latencies is not guaranteed to be one-sided on unseen combinations of batch size and context length. The 'maintaining strict QoS guarantees' property of dynamic chunking is empirical, not structural. TBT violations remain bounded only where the predictor's bias stays on the safe side, so the safe side must hold for the tightest-slack batches. The <10% error figure is stated for chunk size, not as a one-sided bound on batch latency.
conditions: The predictor was profiled on the deployed model, hardware and parallelism configuration.
Serving-time batch compositions lie within the profiled range.
Slack is small enough that a ~10% error can exceed it.

findings.claim: The paper states the predictor's accuracy as a chunk-size error margin, but the safety constraint is a per-iteration batch latency bound (TBT). The paper never gives the relation between the two or any latency-error statistic.
findings.mechanism: A random forest regresses batch execution time. The chunk size is then obtained by inverting that time model against the slack budget. How much a given chunk-size error moves latency depends on the local slope of latency in chunk size, which grows with attention and context length. Average error margins do not bound tail errors. A 10% chunk-size error can correspond to a latency error larger or smaller than 10%, depending on batch composition. Tail behavior under contention or kernel variance is not characterized. The under-prediction bias helps only if the error is mostly one-sided.
conditions: The error margin is a typical-case figure, not a per-batch worst case.
Latency is sufficiently nonlinear in chunk size or context length that chunk-size error maps to larger latency error.
Over-prediction cases exist despite the bias.

findings.claim: The latency predictor is trained from per-configuration offline profiles. The appendix says clock locking is needed for reproducible measurements, so the predictor's validity plausibly depends on the clock state and kernels used when profiling. The paper does not say whether this holds in deployment.
findings.mechanism: Kernel execution time depends on GPU clock frequency, thermal state, kernel implementation and batch composition. A regression model trained on one operating point does not carry to another unless that variation is covered by the training data. If clocks are unlocked or kernels differ from the profiled ones, the predictor's error can exceed the quoted 10% margin. Because the system enlarges chunks specifically when slack is available, such errors would matter most at exactly the iterations where chunks are enlarged. The recurring profiling cost per model, hardware and tensor-parallel setting is also shifted to operators.
conditions: Deployment GPU clocks, thermal state, or kernels differ from the profiled ones.
The training data does not span the shifted regime.
The under-prediction bias is smaller than the induced shift.

findings.claim: The paper defines non-interactive priority with the TTLT deadline plus alpha*(prefill+decode). The Algorithm 1 comparator uses arrival_time + TTFT_SLO + alpha*rem_prefill_tokens for every job. The text does not say which form is implemented, or how non-interactive jobs, which have no TTFT SLO, are keyed.
findings.mechanism: A priority queue orders requests by whatever key the comparator computes. If the key omits the TTLT deadline and the decode term, 600s and 1800s tiers are not distinguished by their deadlines. If the comparator is literal, a non-interactive job's TTFT_SLO is undefined or a placeholder, and the decode estimate of Eq. 5 never enters the ordering. Either the pseudocode is simplified or the evaluated ordering differs from Eq. 5. The origin of the discrepancy is unexplained. No code excerpts were provided to resolve it.
conditions: Algorithm 1 is a faithful description of the implemented comparator.
Non-interactive requests have TTFT_SLO unset, as Table 3 shows.

findings.claim: The decode-length estimate used in the non-interactive priority (Eq. 5) and in the relegation test is a statistical margin over per-application history. It can still under-estimate the remaining work of long-decode requests when the output-length distribution is heavy-tailed.
findings.mechanism: A bound of mean plus k standard deviations is a coverage rule that holds for light-tailed or near-Gaussian data. For skewed, heavy-tailed data, standard deviation is dominated by the tail, and the share of requests above the bound depends on the distribution's shape. The paper states only 'two standard deviations'; the mean offset is not spelled out in the quoted text and is inferred here. The paper's Table 2 reports Azure Conv decode p50 of 41 against p90 of 342, which is strongly skewed. A fraction of requests will therefore exceed the estimate, and for those the Decode_rem term in Eq. 5 under-states the true remaining time. The paper's claim of 'sufficiently captures' therefore rests on TTLT slack being large, not on the estimate being a bound.
conditions: The decode-length distribution of the application is skewed or heavy-tailed.
A non-trivial fraction of requests exceed the estimate.
TTLT slack is small relative to the under-estimated decode time.

findings.claim: The decode estimate is built from a running history per application. That is only a good predictor of the next request if the application's output-length distribution is stationary. A prompt-template change, a model change, or a mixture of short and long modes breaks that assumption, and mis-estimation then feeds both priority ranking and eager relegation.
findings.mechanism: Estimators built from a history window lag behind a distribution shift. A mean-plus-SD summary of a bimodal distribution describes neither mode well. In the evaluation, applications are created by splitting each dataset into three parts, so each 'application' is a sample from one trace distribution. Stationarity therefore holds by construction, and the evaluation does not test the failure mode.
conditions: The application's output-length distribution changes or is multi-modal.
The history window is slow to adapt, or the summary statistic is insensitive to the mode change.
TTLT slack is not large enough to absorb the error.

findings.claim: The paper presents relegation as 'eventual completion without permanent rejection'. That guarantee only holds if load dips below capacity often and long enough to drain the relegated queue. If overload persists, relegated requests can wait indefinitely, which is de facto rejection.
findings.mechanism: A queue served only with spare capacity drains only if the arrival rate averaged over the relevant window is below capacity. Relegated jobs are also ordered behind every non-relegated job. Algorithm 1's comparator places non-relegated jobs strictly ahead of relegated ones. Relegated requests therefore receive only the capacity left after all fresh work. If lower-load periods are absent, rare, or filled by newly arriving requests, 'eventual' has no time bound. The evaluated diurnal trace swings between QPS 2.0 and 5, so it contains low-load troughs. The reported maximum relegated latency of 3900s comes from that trace and does not show behavior under sustained overload.
conditions: Offered load stays above capacity for a long window
Non-relegated requests keep strict priority over relegated ones (drop_status is the first comparator key)
No separate aging or timeout mechanism exists outside the excerpt

findings.claim: The paper says relegation targets requests 'that we know will miss their deadlines'. The operative rule is a binary test for violation 'in the current iteration', and WILL_VIOLATE is not defined in the text. This is a weak proxy for eventual violation of a multi-chunk request. Algorithm 1 also pushes a violating job back and continues, which may not terminate if all queued jobs are relegated and violating.
findings.mechanism: A multi-chunk prefill or a long decode can still meet its deadline even if one iteration looks tight. Conversely, a request can be doomed several iterations before the check fires. A loop that re-pushes the top element and continues, without consuming budget, makes no progress if the same element stays on top. The test's definition and horizon are unspecified, so relegation accuracy is unknown. This could cause relegation of requests that were still salvageable, or too-late relegation of doomed ones. In Algorithm 1, a relegated top job that still satisfies WILL_VIOLATE is pushed back, and the prefill_token_count is not updated. If no non-relegated job is left, the while loop would not advance. The paper may handle this outside the shown pseudocode, which the excerpt does not show.
conditions: WILL_VIOLATE uses only a current-iteration horizon, as the paper's wording suggests
No other exit or fallback exists outside the displayed pseudocode for an all-relegated violating queue

findings.claim: The mechanism moves nearly all violations onto low-priority users. The paper says they eventually complete, but completion is opportunistic, and the reported 3900s maximum is one observation from one trace rather than a bound. The net benefit to the low tier is not quantified.
findings.mechanism: If requests are served only when load is low, their wait is set by how long overload lasts. Sustained overload, or a trace with fewer troughs than the 15-minute 2 QPS phases, would stretch the wait without any scheduler-imposed limit. The diurnal trace returns to 2 QPS every 15 minutes, so relegated work gets regular drain windows. The paper reports a maximum relegated-request latency of 3900s there. With longer or deeper overload, relegated requests would wait longer, and the paper gives no cap. Whether this trade is acceptable depends on business value, which the paper does not measure. The 3900s figure is also well above the Q3 TTLT SLO of 1800s.
conditions: Overload is transient and periodic, as in the diurnal trace
Relegated requests are not starved by later arrivals
The relegated queue is served when load drops

evidence.support_description: ensuring eventual completion without permanent rejection
For relegated requests in QoServe, the maximum latency observed was no more than 3900s

findings.claim: Tbase pruning shrinks only the MILP, which already solves in seconds. It cannot reduce the profiling cost, which is set by candidate generation and by deduplication of repeated chunk specifications.
findings.mechanism: Discarding a pair because its profiled cost exceeds Tbase requires that cost to have been measured already. The decision therefore comes after the expensive step. Pruning acts only after profiling, so it removes MILP variables but not profiling work. Table 4 shows all MILP solves take 0.34-4.22 s, versus profiling that peaks near 3,050 s. The tractability benefit of pruning is therefore small compared with the cost it does not touch, and the profiling budget depends on K and on structural deduplication.
conditions: Pairs are pruned only after their post-overlap cost has been profiled.
Profiling time dominates solve time in the target configuration.

findings.claim: The backbone-first alignment is computed from offline-profiled stable durations. At runtime, the Dynamic Bubble Optimizer moves only movable tasks and leaves the planned backbone order unchanged. Routing skew can therefore turn the statically chosen gap-fit alignment into a suboptimal one that nothing corrects.
findings.mechanism: A gap-fit heuristic's choices depend on the durations of the tasks it aligns. If MoE kernel durations shift per iteration, the best backbone interleaving can shift too. Static planning uses durations from an offline profile, and §6.4 isolates static plans with a mock router that uniformly distributes tokens. §3.2 says routing changes task durations and shifts idle slots in ways no static plan can predict. Only movable tasks such as Wgrad are re-placed at runtime, so any mis-alignment among backbone tasks from the fixed list-scheduler order persists. The 'within ~1% of ILP' result is evaluated on profiled durations only, not on this runtime regime.
conditions: Task durations used by the scheduler come from offline profiles under assumed routing
Backbone order is fixed after static planning
Runtime duration variation is large enough to change the best alignment

findings.claim: Choosing inter-microbatch coupling moves the difficulty from kernels to the planner. Which chunks pair up depends on the partition, and the post-overlap cost of each pair can only be known by scheduling it and measuring it on hardware. This produces the partition-overlap cycle that the paper then has to resolve. Intra-microbatch fusion would not create this cycle.
findings.mechanism: When overlap partners come from different chunks, partition boundaries decide which pairs co-execute. The cost of a stage then depends on its partners and cannot be summed in isolation. The cyclic dependency and the profiling and MILP machinery follow from the inter-microbatch design choice. Tessera's planner contribution is partly a cost of that choice, not only a response to heterogeneity.
conditions: Overlap partners are chosen across chunks by the pipeline schedule.
Overlap efficiency varies across pairs, as in heterogeneous layer mixes.

findings.claim: Warmup/cooldown cost is structural to the template, and exposed EP communication in those phases is not recovered by steady-state overlap. If scaling reduces microbatches per pipeline, that fixed share grows. The paper reports no experiment that varies microbatches per pipeline rank at fixed model and template.
findings.mechanism: In interleaved 1F1B the bubble fraction scales roughly as (p-1)/(v·m), where p is the number of pipeline ranks, v the virtual stages per rank, and m the microbatches per rank. Warmup/cooldown work has few concurrent pairs to overlap. The M-divisible-by-K constraint also ties m to global batch size. At larger scale with fewer microbatches per rank, the steady-state phase that Tessera optimizes best shrinks as a share of iteration time, and the template's structural cost grows. Gains from the partitioner and overlap scheduler may then saturate. This is not tested. The paper does not report microbatch counts for the Table 2 workloads, so the effect cannot be checked from the text.
conditions: Microbatches per pipeline rank decrease as scale increases
Warmup/cooldown cost does not shrink in proportion

findings.claim: The 'by construction' bitwise-equivalence argument assumes that moving tasks on the timeline cannot change floating-point accumulation order. Deferred Wgrad tasks run on a separate thread and are placed at runtime. If they accumulate into shared gradient buffers, the accumulation order could depend on timing. The paper's evidence is one deterministic-mode run, not an argument that covers every case.
findings.mechanism: Floating-point addition is not associative. Accumulating partial gradients into a shared buffer in a different order can change the result bitwise. Deterministic mode typically fixes ordering in a given configuration, and what it fixes depends on the implementation. If a deferred Wgrad task and another contribution (for example, another microbatch's Wgrad or a gradient reduction) write to the same buffer, then the time at which each runs could affect the order of accumulation. The paper does not say whether Wgrad accumulation targets are ordered by explicit dependencies or by timing. It also does not say whether the dynamic optimizer's runtime choices were active in the verification run. Without that, 'by construction' is not established for the dynamic path.
conditions: Wgrad or gradient-reduction tasks from different microbatches write to the same buffer
The accumulation order is determined by execution timing rather than by an explicit dependency
Runtime placement of movable tasks varies between runs

findings.claim: Tessera's partition and overlap schedule are chosen from profiled post-overlap costs of pairs in which both chunks run real computation. A shadow action skips computation. When padding places a shadow action opposite a real chunk in an overlap pair, the pair no longer has the profiled compute-communication profile. The plan's steady-state balance and the dynamic bubble optimizer's assumptions may be affected in the padded portion of the iteration.
findings.mechanism: Overlap hides communication behind computation from another in-flight microbatch. A null operation supplies no computation to hide behind and sends only pseudo-tensors. Per-pair cost therefore depends on both sides being real work. For padded slots, the overlap pairs formed with shadow actions were presumably not among those profiled (the paper profiles real chunk pairs), so the plan's cost model does not describe them. Whether this matters depends on where in the schedule the padding lands and on how many such slots exist. The paper does not discuss interaction between padding and overlap-aware planning or the dynamic bubble optimizer.
conditions: Shadow actions are scheduled in positions where they form overlap pairs with real chunks
The execution plan's per-pair schedules were synthesized and profiled only for real chunk pairs
The number of padded slots is non-negligible

findings.claim: The partitioner picks the partition that minimizes the maximum profiled pair cost. The pair costs come from a small reference group, so the selection is only as valid as the profile is representative of production conditions.
findings.mechanism: A MILP that minimizes a maximum over measured edge costs is sensitive to the relative ordering of those costs. Congestion, routing skew, or EP width that differ from the profiling environment can change this ordering. Even a few percent of error on one pair can change which edge is the maximum. A pair profiled as the cheapest or most balanced on the 64-GPU group could run slower under production jitter or skew. The chosen partition would then be balanced against a stale cost table.
conditions: Production network noise or routing skew differs enough from the reference group to change pair costs by more than the gaps between near-maximum edges.
The perturbed pairs lie on or near the bottleneck of the MILP.

findings.claim: The planner's objective covers only the steady-state overlap edges. Warmup and cooldown exposure is outside the optimized quantity, even though the paper shows it is a large part of the residual exposed communication.
findings.mechanism: Interleaved 1F1B has warmup and cooldown phases whose structure depends on the number of microbatches and the stage layout. A fixed per-pair maximum does not model these phases. As the number of microbatches shrinks, their share of the iteration grows. Two partitions with equal steady-state bottleneck cost can differ in warmup and cooldown cost, and the objective cannot tell them apart. With fewer microbatches per iteration, the surrogate will mis-rank partitions more often.
conditions: Warmup and cooldown exposure differs among partitions that tie or nearly tie on the steady-state maximum.
The warmup and cooldown share of the iteration is non-negligible.

findings.claim: The MILP minimizes Tdom, the largest single overlap-edge cost. The authors state that iteration time depends on the full critical path. A partition with the lowest max edge can therefore still have a longer iteration than another feasible partition.
findings.mechanism: A min-max objective over individual edges does not account for how edge costs accumulate along the dependency chain. It also does not account for cross-rank waits, or for warmup and cooldown phases where few edges recur. Two partitions can have the same or a better Tdom and still differ in iteration time. This happens when the non-bottleneck edges, stage imbalance outside the pairs, or the warmup/cooldown path differ between them. The paper reports no check that Tdom ranks candidate partitions in the same order as measured iteration time.
conditions: Candidate partitions differ in non-bottleneck edge costs or in stage-level imbalance.
Warmup, cooldown, or cross-rank waits are a non-trivial share of iteration time.

findings.claim: The overlap graph, the overlap edges, and the steady-state recurrence assumption are all derived from a fixed schedule template. The partition selected for one template is therefore optimal only for that template.
findings.mechanism: In a graph-labeling formulation, the edge set E and the edge costs depend on which operations the schedule places concurrently on a rank. Changing the schedule, the number of virtual stages, or the microbatch regime changes the graph and the costs, so the old optimum is no longer an optimum of the new problem. Template parameters such as virtual stages per rank or the schedule type are outside the joint optimization. A partition tuned for one setting may be suboptimal after such a change. If the number of microbatches is too small for steady-state edges to recur, the surrogate's recurrence assumption also weakens.
conditions: The template change alters which operations overlap on a rank, or changes the number of virtual stages.
The old partition was selected using edge costs from the old template.

findings.claim: Profile-guided pruning is safe only relative to Tbase and to the candidate neighborhood fixed beforehand. The returned partition is optimal only inside that neighborhood around the serial-balanced baseline, not over all contiguous partitions.
findings.mechanism: A MILP only finds the optimum of the candidate set it is given. If candidates are generated by perturbing a baseline, any better partition outside the perturbation radius is never evaluated or profiled. Pruning removes only pairs worse than the baseline, and candidate generation removes everything outside the neighborhood. The reported gain is therefore a lower bound on what the overlap-aware objective could achieve. The paper does not say how close the neighborhood optimum is to the global one.
conditions: The best post-overlap partition differs from the serial-balanced baseline by more than the candidate perturbation range.
No candidate inside the neighborhood has an equal or lower Tdom.

findings.claim: The scheduler, and the ILP it is compared with, optimize a clean two-resource (Comp/Comm) model. The paper itself reports that real execution deviates from that model through SM contention and coarse tasks. Being close to the ILP in measured cost therefore says little about closeness to the best measured schedule.
findings.mechanism: Ranking schedules by a model is reliable only when the model's error is uniform across the candidates being compared. Interference from SM contention depends on which kernels overlap, so it can differ between schedules. Both the heuristic and the ILP are model-optimal, not measurement-optimal. A small heuristic-vs-ILP gap in measured cost shows the two model-derived schedules behave similarly. It does not show either one is near the best achievable measured schedule. If a task mixes comm and compute kernels, the resource model mis-predicts which overlaps are possible.
conditions: Scheduling decisions are made on analytical durations and a two-resource model
Measured interference varies with which tasks are co-scheduled

findings.claim: Tessera reuses post-overlap costs profiled on a 64-GPU reference group for all ranks and replicas with matching GPU type and interconnect pattern. That matching condition does not by itself ensure the costs reflect production conditions such as fabric congestion or non-uniform routing load. The profiled costs drive MILP partition selection, so any bias in them can shift the chosen partition.
findings.mechanism: All-to-All latency depends on live fabric load and on token-routing skew. A dedicated, quiet reference group measures neither of these in the way a production rank experiences them. The cache key as described (device-mesh class, chunk specification, pass directions, topology) does not include congestion state or routing load. A cached cost is therefore a quiet-fabric, uniform-routing measurement. For communication-heavy pairs, A2A time may be systematically underestimated, which can change which edge looks like the bottleneck.
conditions: Production A2A latency or routing load differs from the reference-group conditions.
The difference affects candidate pairs unevenly, enough to change their relative order or the argmax edge.
The MILP's choice is sensitive to those small relative differences.

findings.claim: The paper says chunk-pair profiling is affordable because repeated model structure bounds the number of distinct overlap pairs. The longest reported run is about 3,050 s, and the distinct-pair count depends on structural repetition. The one-hour result is therefore specific to these repetitive Qwen architectures, and its margin is not large.
findings.mechanism: Total profiling time is roughly the number of distinct pairs times the per-pair cost, and the per-pair cost grows with sequence length. The number of distinct pairs grows when more layer types or more varied chunk boundaries create new chunk specifications. The reported worst case is about 85% of an hour. The one-hour claim rests on a pair count of at most 637 for the tested models, and that count depends on repetition. A model with more distinct layer types, more chunks per rank, or a wider candidate neighborhood could push the count up and exceed the budget, forcing the less accurate fallback.
conditions: The target model has more distinct chunk types or candidate stage assignments than the tested Qwen models.
Per-pair profiling cost is similar to that of the tested cases, or grows with sequence length.
The operator treats a roughly one-hour profile as the budget.

findings.claim: The mechanism takes its overlap opportunities from the pipeline schedule, and Tessera fixes an interleaved 1F1B template. With a single pipeline stage, or too few virtual stages, adjacent operations from different microbatches may not exist. The reported evidence comes from interleaved settings only, such as PP=4 with interleave 2 in §6.4.
findings.mechanism: Overlap between microbatches needs two chunks in flight on a rank. That depends on pipeline depth, virtual stage count, and enough memory to hold concurrent activations. The benefit of the approach is conditional on the schedule providing overlap edges. It is not a property of heterogeneous MoE models alone.
conditions: An interleaved schedule with multiple virtual stages per rank.
Memory headroom for concurrent microbatches.
Enough compute per pair to cover the A2A.

findings.claim: Slot sizing combines observed token counts with an offline-profiled schedule. The paper itself reports that the idealized schedule deviates from silicon, so a sizing error can arise that is invisible to the count exchange and is not quantified for DBO.
findings.mechanism: A duration estimate derived from a profile is only as accurate as the profile's match to runtime conditions such as SM contention, kernel versions, and interference. Overestimating a window leads to injecting a task that does not fit, which extends the critical path. The paper reports an average ~5% theory-to-silicon deviation for overlap pairs, and primitive-level profiling reaches 15% in tail cases. The same kind of error plausibly affects slot sizes. No slot-size prediction error is reported, so the margin before a task overruns its slot is unknown.
conditions: Runtime interference or kernel behavior differs from the profiled configuration.
The task selection has no safety margin against estimate error.

findings.claim: The counts-based predictor sees only routing load within an EP group. The paper names network and switch jitter as a persistent additional source of bubbles, and its proposed extension to cover jitter is explicitly not validated.
findings.mechanism: Per-expert token counts carry no information about communication latency variation caused by congestion or switch contention, and EP-local counts cannot reveal cross-group PP stalls. A bubble from such causes appears with no change in the counts. At production scale some idle slots will not be forecast by the count exchange. They are either left unfilled or sized by the unvalidated moving-average predictor, so DBO's reported production gains cover only the routing-induced share of bubbles.
conditions: Jitter or cross-EP-group skew contributes a significant share of the idle slots.
No history-based predictor is enabled.

findings.claim: The slot-fit check `σ.duration ≤ bβ` uses an estimated window. The paper reports no bound on estimation error or on how often a misprediction delays the backbone, so the 'does not stall' goal is only as good as the estimate.
findings.mechanism: A fit check against a predicted window is safe only when the prediction is not larger than the real idle window. Real windows depend on kernel timing, SM contention, and the opposite chunk's token load, which the estimate only partly captures. The estimate is built from the offline-profiled static schedule plus observed token counts. The paper says such theoretical schedule costs deviate from measured overlapped cost by about 5% on average. If the real window is shorter than bβ, a task admitted by the check runs past the window and delays backbone work. The paper gives no frequency or magnitude for this.
conditions: Estimate error is not systematically one-sided toward under-estimation.
Injected Wgrad runs on a path where overrunning the window delays backbone kernels, rather than being fully hidden by concurrency or stream priority.
The tested configuration does not already absorb these delays within the reported net gain.

findings.claim: DBO picks the highest-scored feasible task for each slot independently as slots arrive. It does not optimize the assignment of the whole movable pool to all slots in an iteration, and the paper does not compare DBO's greedy rule with a global solver.
findings.mechanism: Online greedy packing of items into bins of differing sizes can be suboptimal. Taking an item now can remove the only item that would fit a later bin, and urgency terms in the score can override fit. Because the score mixes duration fit with deadline slack, an urgent small task can occupy a large slot that a large, less urgent task would have filled well. A later slot that only the large task fits then stays empty ('the slot remains empty'). The paper's ILP comparison (§6.5) covers the static overlap scheduler, not Algorithm 2.
conditions: Slot sizes in an iteration are heterogeneous.
The movable pool contains tasks of varied duration and deadline.
Score ties or urgency terms can override best-fit.

findings.claim: The cap of 8 limits how many movable tasks can be deferred. It does not by itself fix how many bytes of activations and gradients those tasks keep live, because task sizes can differ. Memory safety then depends on the separate headroom bound and on how the cap was tuned for each workload.
findings.mechanism: A Wgrad task keeps its input activations and gradients alive until it runs, and those tensors differ in size across layer types (e.g., GDN, softmax attention, MoE blocks) and with routed token counts. A count of tasks is therefore not a count of bytes. Eight deferred tasks could hold very different amounts of memory depending on which layers they come from. A count cap that was safe on one model or partition could still permit an OOM on another unless the headroom check is byte-accurate or the cap is re-tuned. The paper's own handling of OOM (a cap 'configured from observed memory headroom') implies per-workload tuning.
conditions: Movable tasks differ in the bytes of activations and gradients they keep live.
The workload runs close to the per-GPU memory limit.
The headroom bound is not enforced in bytes at each deferral decision.

findings.claim: The objective counts requests as binary pass or fail and optimizes the highest rate at which at least 90% pass. It is insensitive to the severity of failures among the other 10%. The system runs plain FCFS, which the authors acknowledge can produce a convoy effect, so some request classes can have very poor latency while goodput is reported as high.
findings.mechanism: A threshold on the proportion of requests meeting an SLO constrains only how many requests violate, not by how much. Under FCFS with heterogeneous request lengths, the requests that wait behind a long job are a systematic subset and not a random one. The 10% of violating requests can be concentrated in a particular class, such as short requests stuck behind long prefills, and can miss the SLO by large margins without lowering the measured goodput. The reported per-GPU goodput therefore does not bound tail or per-class user-visible quality.
conditions: Request lengths are heterogeneous enough to cause convoy blocking
The violating 10% is not randomly spread
The deployment cares about tail severity

evidence.support_description: DistServe operates with a simple FCFS scheduling policy.
In DistServe, the FCFS policy can lead to a “convoy effect”, where longer requests block shorter ones in the prefill stage.
SLO attainment (the proportion of requests that meet the SLOs)

findings.claim: Algorithm 1 admits a parallel config when the sharded weights fit in GPU memory. The paper says decode batch size is bounded by KV-cache memory. A config that passes the weights check can leave little KV room, so a decode goodput estimate that assumes a large batch could be optimistic. The excerpts do not show whether simu_decode enforces a KV-capacity limit.
findings.mechanism: Decode throughput per GPU rises with batch size because decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound. Available KV space equals GPU memory minus weights and activations, so it shrinks as the per-GPU weight share grows. If simu_decode does not cap the batch by KV space, small-GPU-count configs that barely fit the weights can look best on goodput per GPU, because the per-GPU denominator is small. Such configs would have a small real batch and lower real goodput.
conditions: simu_decode does not itself enforce KV-cache capacity.
The decode batch is memory-limited rather than latency-limited at the tested workloads.

evidence.support_description: inter_op×intra_op < C
Post-disaggregation, the batch size for decoding may be constrained by GPU memory capacity, as it is necessary to maintain the KV caches for all active requests.

findings.claim: The paper reuses Lm, a prefill token threshold, as the largest decode batch size without giving a derivation. The decode batch limit may instead be set by KV-cache memory or the TPOT SLO.
findings.mechanism: Lm is a number of tokens in one forward pass, set by where prefill becomes compute-bound. A decode batch size counts requests, each adding one token per step plus a growing KV cache. Decode limits come from memory capacity, bandwidth and latency targets. The paper separately says decode batch size 'may be constrained by GPU memory capacity'. The Lm cap is therefore either not binding, when memory or TPOT limits bind first, or is an arbitrary ceiling, when they permit larger batches. The text does not say which case holds.
conditions: Decode instances run with a configuration where memory or TPOT permits a batch size different from Lm.
Lm is applied as a hard cap on decode batch size.

evidence.support_description: For decoding instances, we set Lm as the largest batch size.
the batch size for decoding may be constrained by GPU memory capacity, as it is necessary to maintain the KV caches for all active requests.

findings.claim: Algorithm 2 builds each candidate as (inter_op, Pp, Pd) from one inter_op value. Table 3 reports different pipeline depths for the two phases of OPT-66B. The paper does not say how Table 3's per-phase TP/PP values map onto Algorithm 2's segment units.
findings.mechanism: In pipeline parallelism, the number of stages is the number of inter-op groups. Prefill and decoding instances can only be paired 'stage by stage' if both have the same number of stages, or if some explicit many-to-one mapping between segments exists. Algorithm 2 enumerates one inter_op and passes it to both phases via config <- (inter_op,Pp,Pd). Table 3 lists OPT-66B ShareGPT as prefill TP=4, PP=1 and decoding TP=2, PP=2 (Appendix B). Unless get_intra_node_configs returns configurations that themselves contain pipeline splits, or segments are defined differently from the text, the reported placement is not directly a point in the described search space. For OPT-175B the shared-stage reading fits, with PP=3 on both sides.
conditions: The Table 3 PP column counts pipeline stages in the same sense as inter_op in Algorithm 2.
get_intra_node_configs returns only TP-style intra-node configs, with no internal pipeline split.
Table 3 was produced by Algorithm 2 and not by a modified or manual search.

findings.claim: The paper argues that for long contexts the relative cost of KV transfer decreases because prefill grows quadratically. Its own appendix model, however, has a linear GEMM term and a quadratic attention term. The transfer-to-prefill ratio falls only once the quadratic term dominates, and this was not measured.
findings.mechanism: A sum of a linear term and a quadratic term behaves approximately linearly until the quadratic part takes over. KV bytes also grow linearly with context. In that intermediate range the transfer-to-prefill ratio is roughly flat, not falling. The appendix model for GEMM latency is proportional to the token count t, and the attention term is proportional to t squared with a small coefficient. Which term dominates depends on hidden size, block size b, and fitted constants C1 and C2. The paper does not report where the crossover lies, and evaluation used at most 2048 tokens due to OPT's positional embedding limit.
conditions: MHA-style KV size per token, not GQA or MQA.
Context lengths in the range where the linear GEMM term still dominates prefill.
Transfer not hidden by overlap or by NVLINK bandwidth headroom.

findings.claim: The placement algorithms size replica counts n and m by dividing traffic rate by a single-instance goodput. This presumes the dispatcher spreads requests evenly. The paper itself states equal dispatch as an assumption in its queueing discussion, but shortest-queue / least-loaded dispatch is not shown to deliver it, and scaling beyond 4 nodes is not tested.
findings.mechanism: Capacity-planning by n = ceil(R / goodput) is valid only if each replica sees about R/n of the load. Dispatch imbalance makes some replicas exceed their goodput while others sit idle, and a central controller's decisions per second grow with replica count. If dispatch is imbalanced (for example, from the queue-count proxy or an undefined decode 'load'), provisioned replica counts can undershoot the SLO attainment target the simulator predicted for one instance. Agreement of simulator and real system in Table 2 does not by itself test this, because the algorithm simulates a single-instance configuration. The paper does not say whether Table 2 runs used multiple replicas or the same dispatch code.
conditions: Deployment has multiple prefill or decode replicas
Dispatch imbalance is large enough to push some replicas above single-instance goodput
Operating point is near the 90% attainment boundary where small shifts matter

findings.claim: Algorithm 1 and the Figure 1 arithmetic combine separately measured per-phase goodputs, each at 90% attainment. A request must satisfy both SLOs, and the combined system's joint attainment and transfer or queuing effects are not measured in that arithmetic.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: if a request needs both its TTFT and its TPOT to be within SLO, joint attainment is bounded by the per-phase attainments and can be lower than each of them. Combining separately measured goodputs also ignores the interaction between the two pools. Algorithm 1 selects the prefill and decode configurations independently, using simu_prefill and simu_decode, and then replicates them. Each phase is therefore tuned to its own 90% target. The Figure 1 figure is stated as 'Ideally', and its inputs are separate per-phase curves for single GPUs. It is not a measurement of the combined 3-GPU system.
conditions: Algorithm 1 (high node-affinity) is the one used.
Per-phase goodput is measured at a 90% target for each phase separately.

findings.claim: The reported negligible transfer cost (<0.1% of latency) holds because the low node-affinity algorithm keeps KV transfer on intra-node NVLINK. The paper's own bandwidth arithmetic shows the 25Gbps cross-node link would be far too slow for the stated load.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: network transfer cost scales with KV-cache bytes per request and with request rate, and falls back to the slowest link on the path if placement cannot confine it to a fast one. The testbed's cross-node bandwidth is 25Gbps, below the 90Gbps the paper computes for 10 rps with OPT-66B. The low measured transfer share therefore depends on Algorithm 2 keeping prefill and decode segments of the same stage on one node. If a model, GPU count per node or memory budget prevents that colocation, KV traffic would cross the slow link. Savings from removing interference would then be offset by transfer delay.
conditions: The cluster has low cross-node bandwidth.
Prefill and decode segments of the same stage cannot all be placed on one node.
The KV size is large (MHA, long prompts) and the request rate is high.

findings.claim: The paper uses per-GPU goodput at a 90% SLO-attainment target as a direct proxy for cost per query and states 'up to 7.4× lower cost per LLM query'. That conversion holds only if the number of provisioned GPUs is the sole cost. The 90% target also does not guarantee SLO satisfaction for every request.
findings.mechanism: Serving cost in general includes other components such as heterogeneous GPU prices, idle capacity, networking and CPU. A rate-ratio improvement measured per GPU becomes a cost-ratio improvement of the same size only if cost is strictly proportional to GPU count. The paper's cost claim depends on counting GPUs only. Disaggregation holds a separate copy of the weights for each phase and sizes replicas by rounding up, which can leave capacity idle. The cost-per-query ratio can therefore differ from the goodput ratio. Because 90% attainment is the target, 'guaranteed satisfaction of SLOs' can hold at most for the fraction of requests that meet the SLOs, not for all requests.
conditions: Cost is dominated by GPU count
GPUs are homogeneous
Replica rounding waste is small relative to the load
Meeting the SLO for 90% of requests is acceptable service quality

evidence.support_description: higher per-GPU goodput directly translates into lower cost per query
resulting in up to 7.4× lower cost per LLM query with guaranteed satisfaction of SLOs
each phase manages its copy of the model weights

findings.claim: Algorithm 1 sizes prefill and decode separately, each at the SLO attainment target in its own metric (TTFT or TPOT). Requests must meet both SLOs, so the replicated system's joint attainment can fall below the target. Adding headroom to restore it costs extra GPUs, which cuts into the per-GPU goodput the algorithm is meant to maximize.
