The number of such groups is large enough to affect output error

evidence.support_description: Scaling up a single element w usually does not change the maximum value from the group w.
the ratio is larger than 1 for 21.2% of the channels under s = 4

findings.claim: The mechanism avoids a mixed FP16/INT4 format by moving the compensation s^-1 onto the activations. The paper supports hardware-friendliness only through the statement that this inverse scale 'can usually' be fused. For input channels with no fusable predecessor, the hardware benefit is not established by the paper.
findings.mechanism: A scale on the input activations of a linear layer is free only if some earlier operator (for example a norm layer or a linear layer's output) can absorb it into its own parameters. Otherwise it is a separate elementwise multiply executed at inference time. Where no such operator exists, the equivalent transformation still keeps a uniform low-bit weight format but adds runtime work and a kernel launch. The paper's argument for hardware-friendliness over mixed precision then weakens for those layers. The text does not say which layers or architectures fall into this case.
conditions: A preceding operator exists whose parameters can absorb s^-1.
The scaled input channels all pass through that operator.

findings.claim: The closed-form ratio (Δ'/Δ)·(1/s) describes the relative rounding error of one scaled weight element. By itself it does not predict whether the output error of the layer or model falls, because output error also depends on the other elements in the group and on how Δ moves.
findings.mechanism: In absmax group quantization, Δ is shared by every element in a group. Any change in Δ changes the rounding error of all those elements, and output error sums contributions across elements and channels. The ratio 1/s is a motivating quantity for one element under Δ'≈Δ. A monotone benefit in s for the whole network does not follow from it. The paper itself says non-salient channels must be considered separately.
conditions: Δ' ≈ Δ holds for most groups
Non-salient elements contribute little extra error

findings.claim: The Δ'≈Δ step is justified for scaling a single element. In practice about 1% of input channels are scaled together, so a group can contain several scaled elements. Table 2 shows that the share of groups with changed Δ rises quickly with s.
findings.mechanism: A group's absmax can only stay fixed if no scaled element becomes the new maximum. The chance of a changed maximum rises with the number of scaled elements and with s. The single-element argument is an approximation that gets worse as s increases or as more channels fall in one group. The paper's own statistics (Δ changes in 8.2% of groups at s=2 and 21.2% at s=4) show this.
conditions: Scaled channels are small relative to the group maximum
s is modest (the paper says the changed share is small for s < 2)

findings.claim: The α search is driven by a per-layer output-difference objective (Eq. 4). It never directly optimizes final perplexity or task quality, so a lower local error need not translate into a better final model.
findings.mechanism: Quantization errors from successive transformer layers interact and compound through the network. A per-layer objective can be minimized at every layer without minimizing the loss of the full model. The selected α is the best of 20 grid points for each layer's local error on cached calibration inputs. Nothing in the objective constrains the cross-layer accumulated error, so the final-perplexity gap is not controlled by the search. The paper's own Table 3 shows the search does not always reach the mixed-precision reference: at OPT-13B, AWQ is 10.56 against 10.43 for 1% FP16.
conditions: Layer-wise errors interact non-additively across depth
The local optimum α differs from the α that is best for the downstream loss

evidence.support_description: minimizes the output difference after quantization for a certain layer

evidence.location: Table 3 caption (OPT 1.3B-30B rows give the numbers used)
evidence.support_description: achieves comparable performance as mixed-precision (1% FP16)

findings.claim: The search fixes the scale shape to s = sX^α and tunes only one exponent per layer. Every channel is therefore forced onto a one-parameter family tied to its mean activation, even though the scale is applied per channel.
findings.mechanism: A one-dimensional family of per-channel scales is a strict subset of all per-channel scale vectors. Its optimum is generally no better than, and often worse than, the optimum over the full space. The paper's Eq. 5 restricts search to α in [0,1] with a grid size of 20. The best α is a compromise across channels with possibly different saliency and quantization-error tradeoffs. Per-channel or per-group exponents are not tested, so any gain from them is unmeasured.
conditions: Optimal exponents vary across channels or groups within a layer
The layer's error is sensitive to that variation

evidence.support_description: we use a single hyper-parameter α to balance between the protection of salient and non-salient channels
We used a grid size of 20 to search for the optimal α in Equation 5.

findings.claim: The scale family is built from the per-channel average activation magnitude. A channel that is important because of rare large activations could be under-scaled, because its mean is small.
findings.mechanism: A mean over calibration tokens can hide sparse, high-magnitude spikes. Importance for model output may depend on such spikes rather than on the mean. The search can only choose how aggressively to apply the mean-based ordering through α. It cannot reorder channels or give a rarely active channel a larger scale than a frequently active one. The error objective is evaluated on actual X, which can partly reveal damage, but the candidate scales remain mean-based.
conditions: Some channels are important mainly through rare large activations
The calibration set contains or misses those events in a way that makes the mean misleading

evidence.support_description: sX is the average magnitude of activation (per-channel)
It has minimal reliance on the calibration set since we only measure the average magnitude per channel

findings.claim: The paper adds weight clipping 'to minimize the MSE error of quantization' on top of the scale search. The scale search itself targets output difference (Eq. 4). Weight-space MSE and output error are different objectives, so a clip that lowers MSE is not guaranteed to lower output error. In particular, it can cut outlier weights that multiply large activations, which is the case the paper's activation-aware argument says matters most.
findings.mechanism: Output error is the sum over input channels of weight error times activation. A weight-space MSE treats all channels equally and ignores activation magnitude. Clipping an outlier weight adds a large error on that weight, which is exactly the error that large-activation channels amplify. If the clipping objective is computed on weights, it could remove a salient outlier weight, lowering weight MSE while raising output error. This would work against the activation-aware principle. The paper does not say whether the MSE is taken on weights or on outputs, so this applies only under the weight-space reading.
conditions: The clipping criterion is computed on weights rather than on layer outputs.
The group contains an outlier weight that sits on a high-activation channel.

findings.claim: The scaling analysis assumes scaling one element does not change the group maximum, so Δ′≈Δ. Clipping directly changes the group maximum and therefore Δ. The text does not say whether clipping is applied before or after scale search, so it is unclear whether the derived error ratio Δ′/Δ·1/s still describes the deployed quantizer.
findings.mechanism: In absmax quantization, the step size Δ is set by the largest-magnitude weight in the group. Clipping lowers that maximum, so Δ shrinks, and scaling then interacts with the new Δ. If scales are searched on unclipped weights and clipping is applied afterward, the chosen α was optimized for a different Δ than the one used at inference. If clipping comes first, the Δ′≈Δ analysis applies to the clipped weights. The text does not say which order is used.
conditions: The clip is applied to groups where the maximum weight is reduced.
The scale search was run on a different weight state than the deployed one.

findings.claim: The case for weight-only 4-bit quantization is derived entirely in the batch-1, single-stream generation regime. The paper shows no analysis or measurement of how the benefit changes once batching or long prompts raise arithmetic intensity.
findings.mechanism: In a matrix-vector product each weight is read once per token, and with batching each weight read is reused across the batch. FLOPs per weight byte therefore grow roughly linearly with batch size, and a workload leaves the memory-bound regime once its intensity passes the device ridge point. Dequantization adds compute per weight, which is hidden behind memory time only while the kernel stays memory-bound. Above some batch size or prompt length, memory traffic stops being the bottleneck. Weight-byte savings then buy less, and dequantization compute may become exposed. The paper's 'weight access dominates' conclusion is a batch-1 statement.
conditions: Batch size is 1 and generation is single-stream.
Dequantization compute fits under memory time.
Activation and KV-cache traffic stay small relative to weight traffic.

findings.claim: Fusion removes the intermediate FP16 weight write to DRAM. It does not by itself ensure lower latency, because the per-weight ALU work stays in the main loop and costs about three times the useful FMA.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: a kernel's latency is set by the slower of memory traffic and arithmetic. Trading bytes for extra instructions only helps while the arithmetic fits inside time already spent waiting on memory. Fusion lowers the memory term and raises the ALU term. The net effect depends on whether the added instructions stay hidden under the memory time. The paper reports speedups only where the kernel is memory-bound.
conditions: The workload is memory-bound with spare ALU capacity.
Dequantization instructions overlap with memory loads in the main loop.

findings.claim: The paper derives a roofline bound of about 4x for W4A16. Because dequantization must sit in the main loop and costs extra instructions, the realized speedup depends on weight layout and instruction set. It is not fixed by the 4x byte reduction.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: the roofline bound assumes traffic is the only cost. Any added instruction work in the main loop lowers the achievable fraction of that bound, especially on narrow-SIMD CPUs. Fused dequantization is coupled to the packing layout. The paper's own CPU example needs a platform-specific layout (reported up to 1.2x) to cut unpacking to three SIMD instructions per 32 weights, versus three per weight in conventional packing. The fused kernel's benefit is therefore not a property of fusion alone.
conditions: A device-specific offline reordering is available.
The kernel is memory-bound enough to hide the residual unpacking cost.

findings.claim: The packing order is tied to each device's SIMD width, and the GPU uses a different order from the ARM NEON one. A weight file packed for one platform therefore cannot be loaded directly on another. The AWQ quantization step is device-independent, but the packed layout is not.
findings.mechanism: A packed layout fixes which weight index sits in which register lane and nibble. A kernel that unpacks with a fixed mask and shift pattern is only correct for the layout it was written for. The NEON order (w0, w16, w1, w17, ...) differs from the GPU order (w{0,2,4,6,1,3,5,7}). A file packed for one cannot be fed to the other's kernel without an offline repack. The number of stored layouts, or repack runs, then grows with the number of target platforms.
conditions: Target devices differ in SIMD register width or in the kernel's expected order
The fast unpack kernel assumes the packed order and has no layout-agnostic fallback

findings.claim: The paper gives a rule for choosing the index offset for any 2^n-bit register. The mechanism is built and described for 4-bit weights, where two weights share a byte and an AND/shift extracts each. The paper also uses INT3 for quantization quality, but its packing and unpack description is only for 4-bit. Extending to INT3 or other non-power-of-two widths is left unaddressed.
findings.mechanism: A nibble layout gives byte-aligned halves, so one mask and one shift separate the low and high weights. Bit widths that do not divide a byte evenly (such as 3) put weights across byte boundaries, so the same AND/shift pattern does not extract them. The offset rule is derived from 8-bit lanes holding unpacked 4-bit values. It specifies where weights go within registers but does not address non-nibble widths. The paper states TinyChat is for 4-bit models, so INT3 models would not get this fast path as described.
conditions: Weights are stored at a width that divides a byte evenly, as 4-bit does
The kernel unpacks with AND and shift on byte-aligned lanes

findings.claim: The paper's justification for fusion is that individual FP16 kernels on the 4090 take about 0.01 ms, comparable to launch overhead, in a batch-1 decode benchmark. That justification is specific to this regime, and the same fusion should help less once per-kernel compute time grows.
findings.mechanism: Launch overhead is roughly a fixed cost per kernel call, while kernel runtime grows with work. Larger batches or slower devices raise runtime and shrink the launch-overhead fraction. CUDA graphs or similar runtimes can also remove launch cost without fusing kernels. Fusion's relative benefit is largest when kernel runtime is close to launch latency, which holds for tiny batch-1 kernels on a fast GPU. Outside that regime the savings are a smaller share of total latency, so the 1.2x Llama-2-7B fusion gain should not be assumed to transfer.
conditions: Kernel compute time is comparable to launch latency.
The baseline pays per-kernel launch costs without graph capture or equivalent.
Decode is run at small batch size.

findings.claim: The at-most-one-page-group-per-tensor bound, and the background-thread overlap built on it, assume decode produces exactly one token per iteration. Steps that add several tokens could cross page boundaries and need more mappings than the overlap prepared. The paper does not discuss this case.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens per iteration, and chunked prefill processes a block of prompt tokens per iteration. Either can add more tokens than fit in the already mapped page-group. The step API itself takes arbitrary sequence lengths and computes prefill demand as (s+t-1)/t, so it can map more pages. But the decode latency-hiding in §6.1.1 relies on knowing demand one iteration ahead from a single-token increment. A larger step could make the next iteration's mappings fall back to the synchronous path, which costs about 5 ms per request for Yi-34B.
conditions: The serving framework runs multi-token steps in decode-like iterations
The added tokens cross a page-group boundary

findings.claim: Deferred reclamation defers the unmap and release work rather than removing it. The paper triggers reclamation only below a threshold and delegates it to a background thread. Near serving capacity, idle pages held in finished slots reduce free memory for admission, so reclamation is more likely to run during load. The paper gives no evidence on whether that work stays hidden.
findings.mechanism: Memory held in cached slots is unavailable for other allocations until reclaimed. Unmap plus release at 2MB costs about 34µs + 23µs per call (Table 3). A step that needs memory must wait if the background thread has not freed it yet. Under memory pressure the reclamation cost returns, and it is multiplied across 2N tensors. If the background thread lags, the cost can surface as a latency spike in the step that needs the memory. The paper evaluates a single 16K prefill and does not test this regime.
conditions: Cached idle page-groups approach the reclamation threshold under load
The background thread is slower than the demand for freed memory
A step must wait for reclaimed memory before it can proceed

findings.claim: Keeping the KV cache virtually contiguous with on-demand physical mapping only reduces fragmentation if the physical page-group is small. With stock CUDA VMM (2MB pages), each of the 2N per-layer K/V tensors still wastes a partially filled large page per request. The paper's own batch-size result shows this cost.
findings.mechanism: A virtual tensor backed by fixed-size physical pages wastes, on average, part of the last page of every request's sub-tensor. Waste per request therefore scales with page size times the number of independently backed tensors (2N), not with the number of requests alone. The 'no fragmentation' property comes from decoupling plus small page-groups, not from decoupling alone. Without the modified driver (64KB to 256KB), stock CUDA 2MB pages leave much of the fragmentation problem in place, and the paper itself reports lower max batch size with 2MB pages than with 64KB pages.
conditions: Physical backing granularity is 2MB (stock cuMemCreate)
The workload is memory-capacity-limited so that wasted pages reduce batch size
Per-layer K and V remain separate virtual tensors

evidence.support_description: Use of large pages can waste physical memory due to internal fragmentation.
In contrast, 64KB pages helped serve batch sizes of up to 240, 258 and 68 for our models as shown in Figure 15.
Therefore, we implement a new set of APIs in the open-source NVIDIA drivers to mimic the same functionality that existing CUDA APIs provide but with support for multiple page sizes.

findings.claim: The design reserves virtual space of 2N x B x S per worker up front, with S computed at the model's maximum context length. The paper's 'always plentiful' conclusion rests on one configuration. It mixes per-process and total address-space figures, so the margin shrinks as B, N, H or L grow.
findings.mechanism: A process has a fixed user virtual address range (128TB on a 48-bit system). Reservation size scales linearly with batch size B, layer count N, KV heads H, head dimension D and context length L. Worker processes do not pool each other's address space. The paper compares the per-worker 12TB requirement with a 256TB 'total' across two TP workers. The binding limit for a reservation inside one process is that process's own user range, not the sum over workers. The statement that available space 'grows with the number of workers' therefore does not widen the per-worker margin.
conditions: Each TP worker reserves its virtual tensors inside its own process address space
Reservation is sized at maximum context length for all B slots
The user-addressable range is about 128TB per process

evidence.support_description: However, this is not an issue since virtual memory is abundant, e.g., modern 64-bit systems provide a 128TB user-addressable virtual memory per process.
Therefore, the total virtual memory requirement for 60 layers is 120 buffers of 100GB each (12TB total).
e.g., with two TP workers, the total size of user-addressable virtual address space is 256TB.

findings.claim: The paper concludes that virtual memory is always plentiful for the 2xN pre-reserved buffers. The only support is one worked example (Yi-34B, TP-2, B=500, L=200K, 12TB per worker). The reservation grows linearly in B, L, N, H, D and P, so the per-process address-space limit can be exceeded by longer-context or larger-batch configurations. The argument that address space 'grows with the number of workers' does not obviously relax the per-worker budget.
findings.mechanism: Each worker pre-reserves its own 2N buffers, each of size B*L*H*D*P. A single process has a finite user-addressable virtual range (128TB per the paper's own footnote on 48-bit addressing). The total reservation is linear in L and B. If each TP worker is a separate process (an assumption; the paper does not say), its per-process budget is what matters, not the aggregate across workers. The 12TB example uses about 9% of 128TB. Scaling L or B by roughly 10x would exhaust it.
conditions: Per-worker reservation must fit in one process's user virtual range
B and L are set to the maximum values rather than to typical values
Each buffer must remain a single contiguous reservation

findings.claim: Pre-reserving fixed slots of size S per request makes every request's cache live at a stable offset, but it leaves holes when a request in the middle of the batch exits. Kernels must then accept a batch-index indirection between Q and the KV cache (such as FlashAttention's cache_batch_idx). The 'works with unmodified kernels' framing is therefore conditional on that API existing.
findings.mechanism: A request's slot index is fixed by reqId, while its position in the current Q batch changes as continuous batching adds and removes requests. A kernel can read the right slot only if it accepts an explicit batch-index mapping or strided addressing. Contiguity avoids Block-Tables, but the slot layout shifts a compatibility requirement from a paging-aware kernel to a batch-index-aware kernel. Kernels without such an argument would need a copy, a repack, or a code change. This is supported by the paper's own note that FlashInfer lacked stride support.
conditions: Continuous batching creates holes in the slot array
The kernel assumes equal Q and KV batch dimensions

findings.claim: Giving kernels ordinary contiguous per-layer tensors does not by itself make every kernel usable. The kernel must also accept a KV batch dimension that is decoupled from Q (cache_batch_idx-style indexing), and, for the optional tensor-slicing variant, strided addressing.
findings.mechanism: Virtual tensors are indexed by a fixed reqId slot, so finished requests leave unused holes in the batch dimension of the KV tensor. Q is packed only for active requests, so kernels must map Q rows to arbitrary KV slots. The transparency claim depends on kernel API features beyond tensor contiguity. A kernel that assumes Q and KV share one dense batch index would need modification or a copy. The 'no kernel rewrite' benefit is therefore conditional on that API support.
conditions: The batch has holes or reordering relative to reqId slots.
The kernel has no cache_batch_idx-like argument.
Per-layer tensors are used with the 2MB or tensor-slicing configuration in a way that needs strides.

findings.claim: vAttention pre-allocates physical pages at init, while activations come from the standard PyTorch caching allocator. The paper does not say how GPU memory is divided between them. If the activation pool is exhausted, an OOM could occur even while vAttention holds free or cached pages.
findings.mechanism: Physical pages taken through the CUDA VMM path and memory taken by PyTorch's cudaMalloc-based caching allocator are separate pools. Neither automatically lends memory to the other. The activation allocator can fail while the KV page pool still has unmapped or cached pages. Activation memory grows with the tokens processed per iteration (for example, large prefill chunks). The paper reports prefill up to 192K, so these configurations evidently fit.
conditions: Pool sizes are fixed or reclaimed only at thresholds.
Activation demand rises beyond the headroom left after the page pool is sized.
Memory is near full utilisation.

findings.claim: The reqId-slot layout leaves holes in the KV batch dimension when mid-batch requests exit. Those holes are only harmless for kernels that can map Q batch indices to arbitrary KV-cache slots. 'Out-of-the-box' support therefore holds for kernels with such an indexing argument, not for every kernel.
findings.mechanism: A kernel that assumes Q and KV share a packed, identically ordered batch dimension cannot address a KV slot at an arbitrary position. It would need either an equivalent indirection argument or a compacted KV layout. The paper states the hole problem and says FlashAttention's cache_batch_idx solves it. The paper's general portability claim therefore depends on a kernel exposing a comparable argument. This dependence is inferred; the paper does not list which other kernels have such an argument.
conditions: The workload uses continuous batching with mid-batch exits, so holes actually occur.
The kernel assumes Q and KV have matching batch dimension and order.
No equivalent index-mapping or stride argument is available.

evidence.support_description: This layout is not supported by implementations that expect the query (Q) and KV cache to be of the same size in batch (𝐵) dimension.
its argument cache_batch_idx allows Q and KV cache to have different batch sizes and also be arranged in arbitrary order
it supports various attention kernels out-of-the-box

findings.claim: A hole left by an exited request stays backed by physical pages under deferred reclamation. The slot design avoids the hole's kernel-layout cost but ties physical memory to idle or reassigned slots until a reclamation threshold is crossed.
findings.mechanism: Physical GPU memory that stays mapped to an inactive slot is unavailable to other slots or to other consumers such as activations. The paper says only that virtual space is cheap, not that retained physical pages are free. Between exit and reclamation, an idle reqId holds physical page-groups sized to the previous request's context length, and a later short request that inherits the slot also inherits those pages. This residual retention is inferred from the deferred-reclamation description; the paper does not measure it.
conditions: Requests have highly variable context lengths.
Reclamation is triggered only below a cache threshold.
Memory pressure is high enough that retained pages matter.

evidence.support_description: vAttention simply defers the reclamation of R1’s page-groups (Figure 5(d)) and assigns R1’s reqId to R2.
we trigger memory reclamation only when the number of page-groups cached in vAttention falls below a certain threshold (e.g., less than 10% of GPU memory).
Note that this approach could fragment and waste virtual memory. However, this is not an issue since virtual memory is abundant

findings.claim: The step API only reports failure when physical pages cannot be mapped. Whether the system then makes progress depends on a preemption policy that the serving framework must supply. The paper describes only a recompute-style default and does not evaluate its cost.
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: a status code of -1 only reports that mapping failed. Progress requires some component to free pages by evicting or recomputing requests, and that choice affects latency, wasted work and fairness. Recompute-style preemption discards KV state that must be rebuilt through prefill. The paper says a framework 'can' preempt, so progress is conditional on that policy existing and choosing victims whose freed pages cover the shortfall. The artifact guarantees contiguity and on-demand mapping. It does not guarantee liveness or bounded cost under memory pressure.
conditions: Memory demand exceeds available physical pages at some iteration
The serving framework's preemption policy is naive, absent, or frees too few pages

findings.claim: The overlap works only while the next iteration's mapping work finishes inside the current iteration. The paper justifies this with a typical iteration latency of 10s-100s of ms. That is a property of the evaluated A100 setups, not of the mechanism.
findings.mechanism: Faster GPUs, smaller models, and higher tensor-parallel degree shorten decode iterations. Per-call driver latency is a CPU and driver cost that does not shrink with GPU speed. If iteration time falls while per-iteration map work stays the same or rises, the margin shrinks. The paper reports H100 throughput in Figure 11 but runs the hiding ablation (Figure 12) only on A100.
conditions: Iteration time is short relative to aggregate map-call time
Several requests need new page-groups in the same iteration

findings.claim: Reusing a finished request's reqId removes prefill-time mapping only when a finished slot is available and already holds enough page-groups. A burst of arrivals, or a new prompt longer than the old slot's context, still requires mapping on the prefill path. Eager allocation is prepared for only one reqId at a time.
findings.mechanism: A reused slot's mapped size equals what its previous occupant reached. A new prompt larger than that needs the difference mapped. A slot can be reused only after some earlier request has exited. The benefit is bounded by how often a slot is available and by the gap between old and new context lengths. Under a burst of simultaneous arrivals, or when prompts are longer than the freed slots, the remaining mapping falls back on the one eagerly prepared reqId or on synchronous mapping.
conditions: Arrival rate is not far above exit rate over short windows
Freed slots hold at least as many page-groups as the next prompt needs
The background thread finishes eager mapping before the next arrival

findings.claim: The paper's 'no TLB thrashing' result for small page-groups rests on the regular access pattern of the tested attention kernels. It is not a general property of 64KB pages, and it was measured on A100 only.
findings.mechanism: TLB reach is entries times page size, so 64KB pages cover 32x less address space per entry than 2MB pages. Whether that matters depends on how much address space a kernel touches within a short window. TLB and page-table geometry differ across GPU generations. By the authors' own attribution, the harmlessness of small pages is conditional on regular, streaming access. A kernel with scattered access, such as sparse or paged-like attention, could exceed TLB reach and lose performance. The A100 result may not carry over to GPUs with different TLB geometry. This consequence is inferred and was not tested in the paper.
conditions: The attention kernel streams through the KV cache regularly.
TLB and page-table geometry resembles the A100's.
Kernel runtime in isolation is the relevant metric.
